findings.description:
ICE PACK TEST

INDICATION: Evaluation of right ptosis.

TECHNIQUE: Crushed ice in a surgical glove applied over the closed right upper eyelid for 2 minutes. Marginal reflex distance 1 (MRD1) measured immediately before and after application.

RESULTS:
  Right MRD1 before application: 0.5 mm.
  Right MRD1 after application (2 minutes): 3.5 mm.
  Improvement: 3.0 mm, lasting about 4 minutes before returning to the pre-test level.

IMPRESSION: Positive ice pack test (improvement in ptosis of at least 2 mm after cooling). Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Positive ice pack test: right MRD1 improved from 0.5 mm to 3.5 mm (3.0 mm) after 2 minutes of cooling

findings.value: Right frontalis, voluntary activation, 20 fibre pairs

output.impression: Abnormal SFEMG of the right frontalis: mean MCD 58 microseconds, increased jitter in 9 of 20 pairs and blocking in 3 of 20. Findings indicate a disorder of neuromuscular transmission.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: AChR binding antibody 2.9 nmol/L (reference <= 0.02) and blocking antibody 34%; TSH 1.7, free T4 and anti-TPO normal
action_criteria.label: Order AChR binding antibody and thyroid function
action_criteria.rationale: Fatigable unilateral ptosis and diplopia: AChR binding antibody (RIA or cell-based assay) first, positive in about half of ocular MG; thyroid function because thyroid eye disease is the main outpatient mimic and thyroid disease coexists with MG (Evoli, Neurol Sci 2019; Jacob, Pract Neurol 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right MRD1 improves from 0.5 to 3.5 mm after 2 minutes of ice
action_criteria.label: Bedside ice pack test of the right ptosis
action_criteria.rationale: Ptosis is the presenting sign; an MRD1 improvement of at least 2 mm after 2-5 minutes of cooling is cheap bedside support for a neuromuscular junction disorder, and is most useful in ocular MG where neurophysiology is often normal.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: RNS normal (maximum decrement 5%, orbicularis oculi 4%); SFEMG of the frontalis abnormal (mean MCD 58 microseconds, increased jitter in 9 of 20 pairs)
action_criteria.label: Order neurophysiology: repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre EMG of a facial muscle
action_criteria.rationale: Neurophysiology supports the diagnosis: RNS including a facial muscle is the initial test but is normal in more than half of ocular MG, and SFEMG of a facial muscle is the most sensitive test when RNS is normal (Jacob, Pract Neurol 2025; Evoli, Neurol Sci 2019).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No anterior mediastinal mass; normal thymic involution for age
action_criteria.label: Order contrast CT of the mediastinum for thymoma
action_criteria.rationale: Mediastinal imaging is indicated in every patient with MG, ocular or generalized, to detect thymoma (Jacob, Pract Neurol 2025).

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start high-dose prednisone (above 20 mg/day) as an outpatient; start low and titrate, because initial steroid-induced worsening can occur.

Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.
Do not take a normal RNS as evidence against MG: RNS is normal in more than half of patients with purely ocular disease.
required_recommendations: Start pyridostigmine 30 mg three times daily and titrate (usually up to 60 mg four to five times daily) to ptosis and diplopia, watching for muscarinic side effects

If ptosis or diplopia are not controlled by pyridostigmine, add low-dose prednisone (for example 10 mg/day, titrated slowly) (Sanders 2016); observational data suggest that it may also lower the risk of generalization

Counsel him that ocular MG generalizes in about half of patients, mostly within 2 years, and review him regularly over that period with instructions to seek urgent care for dysphagia, dysarthria, limb weakness or breathlessness
Offer an eye patch or occlusion for diplopia while symptomatic treatment is titrated
Give him a list of drugs that can worsen MG and check every new prescription against it

avoided_actions.rationale: MG is a disorder of the neuromuscular junction; EEG has no diagnostic role (Jacob, Pract Neurol 2025).
CSF has no role in MG; normal reflexes, no ataxia and no antecedent infection make Miller Fisher syndrome unlikely (Jacob, Pract Neurol 2025).
Brain and orbit MRI is reserved for negative serology and neurophysiology or a central or orbital mimic; here AChR antibodies and the ice pack test are positive (Jacob, Pract Neurol 2025).
FDG-PET has no role in MG; mediastinal CT answers the thymoma question (Jacob, Pract Neurol 2025).
No cardiac symptom or sign; echocardiography is not part of the MG work-up.
No arrhythmia or autonomic symptom; cardiac monitoring is not part of the MG work-up.

accepted: Ocular myasthenia gravis, AChR antibody-positive (MGFA Class I)

differential.key_features: Normal TSH and free T4; no proptosis or lid retraction; the ptosis is fatigable and improves with ice, and the adduction deficit fluctuates, which a restrictive orbitopathy does not do; AChR antibodies positive.

Right ptosis with limited right adduction can mimic a pupil-sparing partial third nerve palsy, but onset was gradual and painless, he has no vascular risk factors, and the deficit is absent on waking, fatigues during the day and improves with ice; AChR antibodies positive.

differential.diagnosis: Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO / mitochondrial myopathy)
differential.key_features: CPEO is slowly progressive, symmetric, and non-fatigable with fixed ptosis; pronounced diurnal fluctuation is incompatible.
MFS is post-infectious with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia; no antecedent infection, normal reflexes, gradual subacute course here.

key_clinical_evidence: In purely ocular MG (MGFA class I) RNS is normal in more than half of patients; SFEMG of a facial muscle is the most sensitive study, and a normal RNS does not exclude the diagnosis.

Positive ice-pack test (improvement of ptosis after cooling) reflects restoration of NMJ transmission with cooled temperature and is ~80% sensitive for ocular MG; it is cheap and requires no specialized equipment.
AChR antibody positivity in ocular MG (~50% sensitivity) confirms autoimmune etiology and identifies patients at higher risk of generalization within 2 years.
Mediastinal CT with contrast is indicated in every patient with MG, ocular or generalized, to detect thymoma; here it is normal.

Thyroid eye disease (TED) is the principal outpatient mimic; TED causes restrictive ophthalmoplegia (not fatigable), proptosis, lid retraction, and is associated with thyroid dysfunction — normal TSH/free T4 and absent proptosis/lid retraction shift the differential strongly against TED.
Fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides, IV magnesium and neuromuscular blockers can worsen MG and should be flagged at diagnosis so later prescribers are warned.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: RNS sensitivity in pure ocular MG is substantially lower than in generalized MG; a normal RNS in the setting of positive AChR antibodies, positive ice-pack test, and classic fatigable ptosis does not exclude ocular MG — the diagnosis is confirmed by serology and bedside testing
red_herrings.data_point: Normal repetitive nerve stimulation (maximum decrement 5%) across orbicularis oculi, deltoid, and trapezius
red_herrings.intended_effect: Agent interprets normal RNS as evidence against MG and abandons the diagnosis or pursues unnecessary further testing before confirming with serology

findings.description:
CT CHEST WITH CONTRAST

Indication: Newly suspected neuromuscular junction disorder; evaluate for anterior mediastinal mass.

TECHNIQUE: Multidetector CT chest with intravenous contrast in the portal venous phase.

COMPARISON: None.

FINDINGS:
Anterior mediastinum: No discrete anterior mediastinal mass. Minimal residual thymic tissue consistent with normal fatty involution for age. No thymic enlargement. No calcification.
Lymph nodes: No mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy.
Lungs: Lung parenchyma clear bilaterally. No nodule, consolidation, or pleural effusion.
Heart and pericardium: Cardiac silhouette within normal limits. No pericardial effusion.
Chest wall and osseous structures: No osseous destruction or suspicious lesion.

IMPRESSION:
1. No anterior mediastinal mass. Appearances are consistent with normal thymic involution appropriate for a 39-year-old male.
2. No mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Lungs clear.

body_imaging.impression: No anterior mediastinal mass. Normal thymic involution for age. No mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Lungs clear.

abnormal_values_summary: AChR binding antibody 2.9 nmol/L (H; reference <= 0.02 nmol/L)
labs.interpretation: AChR binding antibody elevated at 2.9 nmol/L and AChR blocking antibody elevated at 34%. Blood count, metabolic panel, CK, TSH, free T4 and anti-TPO within reference ranges. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are found in about half of patients with purely ocular myasthenia and in most with generalized disease; clinical correlation recommended.

past_medical_history: No prior neurological or autoimmune disease

patient.history_present_illness: A 39-year-old man with no prior medical history presents to the neurology outpatient clinic with a 6-week history of progressive right eyelid drooping and binocular horizontal double vision. He first noticed his right eyelid felt heavy after a long day at work approximately 6 weeks ago. Initially he attributed this to fatigue and sleep deprivation. Over the following 2 weeks the ptosis became apparent earlier in the day and more pronounced by the evening. Three weeks ago he developed double vision — horizontal, worse on left lateral gaze — which also worsened as the day progressed. He reports that both the ptosis and diplopia are essentially absent when he first wakes up in the morning and return progressively throughout the day. He has no headache, no pain behind the eye, no visual acuity change, and no photophobia. He denies any swallowing difficulty, nasal speech, choking, arm or leg weakness, or shortness of breath. He has not had a preceding viral illness, vaccination, or any new medication. His primary care physician tested thyroid function approximately 2 weeks ago (result unretrieved). He was referred urgently to ophthalmology who found normal intraocular pressure, normal fundoscopy, no proptosis, and no lid retraction, and referred him on to neurology for evaluation of the fatigable ptosis.

neurological_exam.additional: No dysarthria or dysphagia. No neck flexor weakness. No respiratory symptoms. No bulbar or limb involvement documented.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Right upper eyelid ptosis, MRD1 0.5 mm right, 4 mm left. Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze: right eyelid descends to cover pupil completely at 35 seconds. Binocular horizontal diplopia on leftward gaze; resolves with right eye covered. Limitation of right eye adduction on left lateral gaze. No proptosis. No lid retraction. Pupils 3 mm, equal, reactive to light. Corneal reflexes intact. Facial sensation normal bilaterally. Facial muscle strength 5/5 bilaterally. Palate rises symmetrically. No dysarthria at rest.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented x4. Language and cognition intact.
neurological_exam.motor: Strength 5/5 in all four limbs. No proximal or distal weakness. No fatigability on repeated limb testing.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 2+ and symmetric. Plantar responses downgoing.

physical_exam.cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs.
physical_exam.general: Well-appearing man in no acute distress. No dysmorphic features.
physical_exam.neurological: Right upper eyelid ptosis, MRD1 0.5 mm (left 4 mm). Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze complete at 35 seconds. Binocular diplopia on left lateral gaze with limited right eye adduction. No proptosis. No lid retraction. Pupils equal and reactive. Facial sensation and motor intact. Palate symmetric. No dysarthria. Strength 5/5 all limbs. Reflexes 2+ symmetric. Sensation intact. Coordination normal. Gait normal.
